# Molecular basis of inheritance: DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation, gene regulation

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Molecular basis of inheritance** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Molecular basis of inheritance: DNA structure
### replication
### transcription
### translation
### gene regulation

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Heredity is chemistry. DNA was found in 1869 (Miescher), shown to be the transforming principle in 1944 (Avery), confirmed by the Hershey–Chase blender experiment in 1952, and its double helix solved by **Watson and Crick in 1953** using Chargaff's base rules and Franklin's X-ray photo. From that structure follow everything: semi-conservative replication, the central dogma DNA → RNA → protein, the genetic code, and gene regulation (the lac operon as the model).

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the experiments that made DNA the genetic material (study in this order)**

| Step | Experiment | Year | What it proved |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Miescher isolates 'nuclein' from pus cells | 1869 | DNA exists as a distinct chemical |
| 2 | Griffith's transformation in pneumococcus | 1928 | A 'transforming principle' passes heritable traits between bacteria |
| 3 | Avery–MacLeod–McCarty | 1944 | The transforming principle is DNA (destroyed by DNase only) |
| 4 | Chargaff's rules | 1950 | A = T and G = C in any species' DNA |
| 5 | Hershey–Chase blender experiment | 1952 | Only the DNA of T2 phage enters E. coli — DNA is the genetic material |
| 6 | Watson–Crick double helix (+ Franklin's Photo 51) | 1953 | Structure suggests a copying mechanism |
| 7 | Meselson–Stahl density labelling | 1958 | Replication is semi-conservative, exactly as predicted |

**DNA vs RNA — classified comparison**

| Feature | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose (no 2'-OH) | Ribose |
| Bases | A, G, C, T | A, G, C, U |
| Strands | Double helix (two antiparallel strands) | Usually single-stranded |
| Stability | Very stable — archival store | Less stable — working copy |
| Location (eukaryote) | Nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts | Nucleus and cytoplasm |
| Types | One (genomic; + organellar) | mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, miRNA |
| Job | Store and transmit heredity | Express it: message, adapter, factory |

**Replication vs transcription vs translation — the three engines of the central dogma**

| Feature | Replication | Transcription | Translation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Template | Both DNA strands | One DNA strand (the template strand) | mRNA |
| Enzyme | DNA polymerase (+ helicase, primase, ligase) | RNA polymerase | Ribosome + peptidyl transferase (rRNA enzyme) |
| Raw material | dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) | NTPs (ATP, UTP, GTP, CTP) | Aminoacyl-tRNAs |
| Start signal | Origin of replication | Promoter + start site | AUG start codon |
| Stop signal | Termination sites | Terminator | UAA / UAG / UGA stop codons |
| Product | Two identical DNA duplexes (semi-conservative) | mRNA (5'→3') | Polypeptide (N→C) |
| Proofreading | Yes — polymerase 3'→5' exonuclease | No significant proofreading | None |
| Where (eukaryote) | Nucleus (S phase) | Nucleus | Cytoplasm, on ribosomes |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — reading the code.** A template DNA strand reads 3'-TAC GGA TTA-5'. The mRNA is 5'-AUG CCU AAU-3' (U replaces T; transcription starts at the promoter, not at AUG by chance). Reading in frame: AUG = methionine (start), CCU = proline, AAU = asparagine — peptide Met-Pro-Asn. Note the logic: complement the template, then translate the mRNA, never the DNA directly.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Describe the Watson–Crick model with base-pairing rules and antiparallel direction. (2) Why is replication called semi-conservative — and how did Meselson–Stahl prove it? (3) List the differences between DNA and RNA. (4) Compare replication, transcription and translation (template, enzyme, product). (5) Explain lac operon regulation: repressor, inducer (allolactose), negative control. (6) Properties of the genetic code: triplet, degenerate, non-overlapping, universal.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** DNA stores information as base sequence; replication copies it semi-conservatively; transcription and translation express it through the central dogma; operons regulate expression. Every hereditary ratio Mendel saw is, at bottom, the chemistry of complementary base pairing. **Self-check:** can you transcribe and translate a 6-base template strand without notes?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: DNA structure in numbers: double helix, antiparallel, 2 nm wide, 3.4 nm per turn, 10 bp/turn; A=T, G≡C (Chargaff) — the numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Replication: semi-conservative (Meselson–Stahl), 5'→3' synthesis, leading continuous/lagging Okazaki fragments, DNA polymerase + helicase + ligase — one line each.
Trick 3: Central dogma: DNA →(transcription, RNA polymerase)→ mRNA →(translation, ribosome + tRNA)→ protein; genetic code: triplet, degenerate, universal, non-overlapping.
Trick 4: tRNA cloverleaf carries the anticodon; Wobble pairs; start codon AUG, stops UAA/UAG/UGA — the code table essentials.
